extracted.intended_audience: students, correspondents, and readers of a 19th-century mathematical problems journal (problem proposers and solvers; geometers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and worked solutions for proposing and solving mathematical exercises (particularly plane and spherical geometry, coordinate-curve representation, and construction of numerical equations). Includes editorial submission requirements for correspondents and methodological advice for students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission requirement: include sketch of intended solution
rubrics_metrics.description: We have particularly to request those correspondents, who favor us with new questions, to accompany them with at least a sketch of the intended solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: A problem may be impossible or an alleged theorem not true, and editors cannot always invest time to investigate questions fully between receipt and publication. Therefore proposers should provide a sketch (diagram/outline) of their intended solution to allow editorial verification and to save editors' time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation convention for iterated trigonometric functions
rubrics_metrics.description: According to the usual functional notation sin² denoting sin. of sin a; sin³ denoting sin. of sin² a.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt the stated functional notation when writing problems/solutions so readers understand iterations of trig functions unambiguously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose coordinate system that simplifies depiction or analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the system of co-ordinates which offers the greatest facilities for depicting equations graphically, or which produces the analytical representation of the figure in its simplest form (or in the form from which its properties may be most conveniently evolved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tasked with producing an equation from a geometric definition, prefer the coordinate system that (a) makes coordinates/simple motions simple (ease of graphical construction), or (b) yields the simplest analytical form for deriving properties. This is a practical criterion for selecting among rectilinear, polar, or other coordinate systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer rectilinear and polar systems for graphical formation
rubrics_metrics.description: The system best adapted for graphical purposes is that by which the curve is generated by the intersection of two right lines having motions of translation parallel to two fixed axes. Another very useful system is that which determines a curve by the translation of a point in a right line revolving about a fixed point or pole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For most elementary graphical work prefer rectilinear (translations parallel to axes) or polar (translation of a point on a line revolving about a pole) because their elements and modes of variation are simplest; these are almost exclusively preferred in elementary analytical geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method: derive equation from definition via primitive equation then eliminate
rubrics_metrics.description: Every definition of a curve that indicates a method of description (by points or continued motion) constitutes a first (primitive) equation relative to an implied coordinate system; write this primitive equation, then eliminate auxiliary variables by relations to the proposed coordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure for producing an analytical equation: (1) write down the primitive equation implied by the curve's definition in the most natural coordinate system, (2) write relations between those primitive coordinates and the target coordinates, (3) eliminate to obtain the desired equation. This is the recommended systematic approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of negative radius in polar coordinates (allow negative r)
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative values of the radius vector in polar co-ordinates should be measured backwards (in the opposite direction) rather than rejected, because rejecting them often deprives curves of branches that appear in other coordinate systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To obtain complete figures from polar equations, accept negative r (measure backwards) as consistent with Descartes' principle that inversion/change of sign corresponds to analytic changes; this also explains the known changes of sign of trigonometrical secant and preserves branches that would otherwise be missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for forming numerical equations with nearly equal roots
rubrics_metrics.description: Find two or more integer numbers whose square roots have several figures in the decimal part common to all the roots; increase or decrease the integer parts of these roots by such arbitrary numbers as will make the roots coincide both in integers and decimals to the same extent; then employ the double sign before the surd part to furnish the several roots of an equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical recipe and example: choose integers whose square roots share decimal prefixes, adjust integer parts so roots agree to desired decimal places, form roots as ±(integer_part ± surd), and construct the polynomial with those roots. Advice: by multiplying by arbitrary integer factors one can increase degree; select examples with small coefficients for practice.
